newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu resurfaces, says his only interest is Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu resurfaces, says his only interest is Zaire.

text.p: Zaire's beleaguered President Mobutu Sese Seko reappeared in public on Sunday for the first time since returning home and said he was back to devote himself to the higher interests of his country and not his own.
Mobutu, looking tired and thin but wearing his trademark leopard-skin hat with a dark suit, was speaking before talks with South Africa's Deputy President Thabo Mbeki.
Mobutu returned from France on Friday, following fresh successes by rebels fighting to topple him. He has spent most of his time in Europe since prostate cancer surgery in August.

"I have returned not to devote myself to Mobutu's interests nor to Mobutu's fortune as you write from time to time but to the higher interests of Zaire," he told journalists. "That is to say our unity, our territorial integrity."
Asked how he felt, Mobutu, who left hospital in Monaco after fresh cancer treatment on Wednesday, replied: "I feel the way I look."

Mobutu, 66, has ruled Zaire since seizing power in an army coup in 1965, but many ordinary Zaireans, ground down by three decades of poverty and hardship under his rule, are eager for a change and are openly rallying to the rebels.

Mobutu welcomed Mbeki with an embrace. Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo joined Mobutu and Mbeki, who was at the heart of a bid by South Africa's Nelson Mandela to broker peace between Mobutu and the rebels last month.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila, his popularity soaring with each new battlefield victory, said on Saturday that he would not work with anyone who had shared power with Mobutu.
Kabila outlined his plans for a transitional government during his first visit to Zaire's third city of Kisangani which the rebels captured on March 15.
He told a news conference a transitional government should include members of his Alliance for Democratic Forces for the Liberation Congo/Zaire (ADFL).
"We say the ADFL transitional government should be made of ADFL members and only anti-Mobutists and anti-regime people who have never been in power and who never shared power," he said.
Any transition, he added, should last no more than a year.
Before leaving France for home, Mobutu called for a truce and talks and the creation of a national council to find ways out of the crisis "with all our brothers, without exclusion".
Kabila and a roaring crowd of 10,000 supporters in Kisangani firmly told U.N. special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun on Saturday there would be no ceasefire with the government before negotiations.
Sahnoun, trying to broker a peace deal, left Kisangani after brief talks with Kabila, whose forces control a fifth of Zaire.

On the war front, rebel Voice of the People radio said on Saturday rebels had pushed south to within 200 km (125 miles) of Zaire's second city Lubumbashi, capital of mineral rich Shaba, and 100 km (60 miles) of the diamond capital of Mbuji-Mayi.
It did not say where exactly they had reached.

The rebels took up arms in October in a dispute about Zairean nationality for an ethnic Tutsi minority, who form the core of Kabila's fighting force. An alliance of anti-Mobutu groups rallied to the cause.

The United States, France and Belgium have sent or are preparing to send troops to countries neighbouring Zaire in anticipation of any need to evacuate their citizens. The first U.S. soldiers left Italy for the region on Sunday.
